Render T112's kernel from T105's, swapping ONE member of the CoAtNet stage for ours.

T111 registered the reading: "our arm swapped for theirs inside the CoAtNet stage at the same weight, everything else byte-identical." This renders exactly that, in scripts/t110/build_t110_kernel.py's idiom -- every edit is an exact string replacement that RAISES when it does not apply, because a patch that silently no-ops scores the unchanged parent and looks like a null result.
That is the defect class this project logs as a check that passes for the wrong reason, and a whole submission rests on the swap actually taking.
WHY native384-v8 IS THE DEFAULT TARGET.
The stage is four views over three files:

maxspan-v5 v5_full_swa.pt _SLOTS64 img 336 k_eval 62 w 0.55 native384dense-v10 v10_full.pt _SLOTS64 img 384 k_eval 62 w 0.10 maxspan-v5-reverse v5_full_swa.pt _SLOTS64 img 336 k_eval 62 w 0.15 native384-v8 v8_full_swa.pt _SLOTS44 img 384 k_eval 42 w 0.20

native384-v8 is the only one framed on _SLOTS44, and _SLOTS44 is the framing our corpus and our trainer already use -- (N, 44, 336, 336), windows of three consecutive slices, eval centres spread over the valid slices.
Swapping it is therefore a ONE-VARIABLE change: same slot layout, same span, same weight, one different set of weights.
Swapping maxspan-v5 instead would move the slot layout and the weight at the same time and confound the answer with the framing.
--replace allows the other choice, deliberately and on the record.
THE THING THAT ALMOST COST A QUOTA KILL, and the reason img defaults to the REPLACED MEMBER'S value rather than to our resolution.
In cell 47 the arms are grouped before inference:

key = (int(arm["img"]), arm["slots"], arm["span"], int(arm["k_eval"])) ... volume, mask = build_study(...) # ONCE per group for arm_index, arm, model, resolution in loaded: windows = eval_windows(volume, mask, k=K_EVAL, res=resolution, ...)

So img/slots/span/k_eval are the decode recipe -- every distinct combination costs a full pass over the test set -- while res, which comes from ck['res'], is applied per arm, after the decode, inside eval_windows.
A 224-trained arm therefore does NOT need img 224: it needs img 384 so it joins native384-v8's existing group, and res 224 so eval_windows hands it 224 px.

The first draft of this builder defaulted img to our resolution, which would have added a fourth decode group to a run T105 measured at 429-434 min against a registered 495-min cap -- about 60 minutes of margin, spent on re-decoding every study for no reason.
assert_decode_group_preserved() now refuses that.
THE DEFECT THAT WOULD HAVE BEEN READ AS A RESULT.
Their eval_windows ends with
and NORM = "imagenet" for every arm.
Our trainer does not normalise at all -- src/coat_data.py divides by 255 and stops.
Measured: their inputs carry ~4.48x our standard deviation and a -0.24 mean shift.
A model trained on [0, 1] and evaluated on that is being fed a different distribution entirely.

What makes this the dangerous kind of bug rather than the loud kind: the kernel runs clean, the VOID banner prints because the arm really did run, and the score comes back low -- which T112's registered rule reads as "<= 0.934 REJECT, our arm is worse than theirs." We would have entered a resolved negative about our own architecture into the record on the strength of a normalisation mismatch.
So the arm carries its OWN norm in the ARMS entry and the call site becomes norm=arm.get("norm", NORM), leaving every other arm on "imagenet" exactly as before.
It is still one cell, because the call site is in this same cell.

So dataset_sources was inherited verbatim, our arm's dataset was never added, and find_weight_file("ours_coat_t112.pt") would raise RuntimeError(... not found under /kaggle/input).

built WITHOUT img_size -> forward 224 FAILS: "The size of tensor a (196) must match the size of tensor b (576)" built WITH img_size=224 -> forward 224 OK

The kernel runs to COMPLETE, the VOID banner prints (it prints at import, before the arms run), and our column stays a constant 0.5 for every study.
A constant column is invariant under the notebook's rank-percentile routing, so the submission is exactly the parent with our member zero-weighted -- it measures the REMOVAL of a member.

Thirteen stages stand between a trained checkpoint and a scored leaderboard submission.
This runs all thirteen, on the REAL corpus and the REAL notebook, with a tiny backbone on CPU so it costs seconds rather than hours -- and prints PASS or FAIL per stage.
THE STAGE COUNT IS GATED, and that is not decoration.

Review on 2026-09-18 caught this script printing nine PASS lines and then dying on a traceback, while the summary being quoted upstream was "passes 9/9" -- which is exactly what you get by reading the PASS lines of a crashed run.
A report that passes for the wrong reason is the same defect as a check that does, one level up.
So EXPECTED_STAGES is asserted, main() catches its own crash and records it as a FAILED stage, and the docstring's count is checked against the code rather than believed.
It is deliberately CPU-ONLY.
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is cleared before torch is imported, for the reason T067 measured on 2026-09-09: a process that claims a CUDA context makes gpu_queue.sh log "GPU busy again;
deferring" and restart a queued fold's full 20-minute cooldown.
This script is meant to be safe to run while a fold is queued behind it.
What it cannot prove: that the arm is GOOD.
Nothing here reads a leaderboard or a gold AUC on a real model.
It proves the plumbing carries water.

The rule for this list is narrow.

A check belongs here only when it needs an artifact that is gitignored and too large or too third-party to track -- the 32-checkpoint outputs/ckpt22 bank, the 533 GB corpus and its teacher, the upstream 0.941 notebook.

Everything else was made environment-independent instead: data/fixtures/t105_arm_reference.json caches the three definitions the export checks execute, and coat_export.arm_reference() REFUSES when the cache and the live notebook disagree, so the fallback covers absence and never disagreement.
These run after the gate, are reported with their own count, and count toward pass/fail exactly as the gated ones do.
What they do NOT do is move the md5, because a hash that depends on which artifacts happen to be on the machine is not an identity.

Registered in deaddrop/tasks/T112-the-4090-first-day.md BEFORE this ran, after review found the gap: the trainer reaches the model's 224 px from the 336 corpus in one bilinear step, while the kernel decodes the DICOM to 384 and then resizes to 224 -- 1.714x non-antialiased decimation against 1.5x.

Three conditions, same checkpoint, same 58 studies, same device and precision:

A 336 -> 224, k 24 what the trainer measured (0.8848 on GPU/bf16) C 336 -> 224, k 42 the kernel's window count, the trainer's resample B 336 -> 384 -> 224, k 42 the kernel's window count AND its resample chain
So C - A isolates the window count and B - C the resample chain.
The registered rule: if |B - A| >= 0.036 -- the gold-58 noise band -- the morning's reading does not predict the kernel and must NOT be used to clear the BROKEN floor for this submission.
What B approximates, stated plainly: the kernel's 384 volume is a direct INTER_AREA decode of the DICOM;
here it is the 336 corpus upsampled to 384 and then downsampled.
That adds an upsampling step the kernel does not have, so B is an approximation of the chain, not a replica of it.
The DICOM path would need the kernel's own decode, which is outside what a 58-study check should build.

Why this exists.
With the Kaggle GPU quota exhausted (T112, 2026-09-18) the leaderboard is closed, and gold-58 is the only truth-anchored instrument left.
Its ABSOLUTE band is +/-0.036 -- too coarse to rank two arms 0.03 apart.
But two models scored on the SAME 58 studies are a paired comparison, and T057 measured gold-58's paired band at +/-0.0044-0.0101.
This script is that paired read, so "our arm trails theirs" stops being two numbers eyeballed across documents and becomes one delta with a confidence interval.
Each model is scored under ITS OWN recipe, because that is how each would run in the kernel:
ours decode 384 -> res 224, norm 'none', k 42 (the native384-v8 slot) theirs decode 336 -> res 384, norm 'imagenet', k 42
For v5_full_swa the 336 corpus IS its decode size, so its chain is faithful.
What is NOT faithful, stated: v5 was trained and deployed on a 64-slot volume with 62 windows;
the corpus holds 44 slices, so it is scored here with 42.
T071 measured the same checkpoint on our 58 at 0.9002-0.9187 depending on crop and slice density, against its own stored 0.9214 -- a reading, not a target.

(model, res, norm) for EITHER key format, read from the checkpoint itself.
A CoatMIL checkpoint (ours) carries head. keys and its recipe;
a RaptorClassifier one (theirs, or ours after export) carries res and, if we wrote it, train_norm.
The model is built as the class its keys belong to, so neither side is forced through a conversion here.
A checkpoint WE trained predates norm in RECIPE if it has no such key, and our trainer then fed [0, 1] -- so our default is "none".
The published member's pipeline applies ImageNet normalisation to every arm.
Encode in chunks, pool over ALL k windows.
Exactly equivalent to one forward: the backbone is per-window and BatchNorm is in eval mode, so no window's features depend on its neighbours in the batch.
Needed because 42 windows at 384 in fp32 do not fit the laptop's 8 GiB.
ours: CoatMIL key names, its recipe carried in the checkpoint
theirs: the notebook's own class, extracted rather than retyped
